what: Loar Holdings makes small, specialised aerospace parts: latches, locks, seals, fluid controls, sensors, cables and similar components. Almost all of them are proprietary designs certified for a specific aircraft, and most of the revenue comes from selling replacements to airlines rather than from building new planes.
customers: Aircraft manufacturers who design the parts in, and then for decades afterwards the airlines, maintenance shops and defence operators who must buy replacements.
money: Replacement parts for aircraft already in service, the highest-margin revenue.
Components supplied to aircraft and engine manufacturers for new production.
Parts for military aircraft and government programmes.
moat: Aerospace parts are approved for one aircraft type and cannot legally be substituted, so the company that holds the certification holds a small monopoly for the thirty-year life of the airframe. Each part is cheap relative to the aircraft and expensive to re-certify, which means nobody bothers competing for it. Loar’s strategy is to buy dozens of these niche positions and raise prices on all of them.
risks: The shares trade at about 105 times earnings, 9.8 times sales and 36 times EV/EBITDA. That is a price that assumes this model works for many years without interruption.
Debt of $722.1M against $84.8M of cash was raised to fund acquisitions, and this strategy only works while acquisitions can be bought at sensible multiples.
The company listed recently, so there is limited public record of how it performs through a downturn or how durable the pricing strategy is under airline pressure.
Airlines and manufacturers are increasingly resistant to above-inflation price increases on parts, and that resistance is the main long-term risk to the model.
Five analysts average an $88.80 target against a $66.25 price, which is thin coverage for a company on this multiple.
opportunities: Revenue has grown very fast, from $317.5M in 2023 to $496.3M in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $635.6M.
The aftermarket is 55% of revenue and grows with flying hours rather than with aircraft orders, which makes it steadier and far more profitable than original equipment work.
Free cash flow of $118.5M on $635.6M of revenue shows the economics of proprietary parts clearly.
The global aircraft fleet is old and airlines are flying existing planes longer because of delivery delays, which raises replacement part demand directly.
There is a long supply of small, family-owned aerospace component makers to acquire, which is the engine of the strategy.
watch: Aftermarket revenue growth and the price paid for each acquisition. The model is sound; the risk is paying too much for the next set of niche positions, and that shows up in the multiple paid per deal rather than in any quarterly figure.
view: Loar is running the TransDigm playbook, and that playbook is one of the most reliably profitable in industrials. The logic is this: a latch on an aircraft door is certified for that specific aircraft, cannot legally be substituted with an uncertified equivalent, costs almost nothing relative to the aeroplane, and will be replaced on a schedule for the thirty-year life of the airframe. Whoever holds the certification holds a small, legally protected monopoly that nobody will spend money to challenge. Collect enough of these, raise prices on all of them annually, and you compound at a rate that looks implausible until you understand why nobody competes.

The aftermarket concentration is what makes it work. Fifty-five percent of Loar’s revenue comes from parts for aircraft already flying, which means demand tracks flying hours rather than aircraft orders. That is a profoundly better business than supplying manufacturers: it is steadier, higher-margin, and currently enjoying a specific tailwind because Boeing and Airbus delivery delays have forced airlines to keep older aircraft in service far longer than planned. Old planes need more parts. Free cash flow of $118 million on $636 million of revenue tells you what the margins on proprietary parts look like.

Now the problem, and it is entirely about price. At 105 times earnings, 9.8 times sales and 36 times EV/EBITDA, the market has already decided this works. TransDigm and HEICO earned their multiples over decades of demonstrated pricing power through recessions, grounded fleets and a pandemic. Loar listed recently and has no comparable public record. Paying a proven compounder’s multiple for an unproven one is how people lose money in good businesses, and the $722 million of acquisition debt against $85 million of cash means the strategy has to keep working on schedule.

There is also a slow-burning risk nobody prices properly: the customers have noticed. Airlines and manufacturers have become markedly more resistant to above-inflation parts pricing, and procurement pressure is the one thing that would break this model. It will not happen in a quarter; it happens over a decade. My read is that Loar is a genuinely good business bought at a price that requires near-perfect execution, with five analysts covering it. I would want the multiple considerably lower, or a longer public record, before paying this. What to watch is not revenue but what Loar pays for each acquisition — the whole return depends on buying niche monopolies cheaply, and the moment it starts paying full price for them the compounding stops.
bull: Aftermarket demand keeps rising as airlines fly older fleets, acquisitions of niche certified positions continue at sensible multiples, and Loar compounds its way into the multiple it already carries.
bear: Acquisition prices rise, airline procurement pushes back on parts pricing, and 105 times earnings with $722 million of debt leaves no room for either.
